cases.abstract: Prediction-set calibration can target the severity of errors, not just whether the correct answer is included. Conformal risk control selects a parameter after correcting the average of n calibration losses for the worst possible loss on an unseen observation. For exchangeable, non-increasing, right-continuous loss functions bounded above by B and with an endpoint loss at most the target alpha, this rule guarantees expected test loss at most alpha. If the functions are also independent and identically distributed, nonnegative, and have zero probability of a jump at any fixed parameter, expected loss is at least alpha - 2B/(n + 1); examples show this general lower bound is sharp. Segmentation, multilabel and hierarchical classification, and question answering illustrate control of nonbinary losses over 1,000 random data splits. The guarantee averages over calibration and test data, rather than certifying risk for every fitted set. Monotonicity supplies the link between parameter selection and risk control: without it, expected loss can approach B despite a lower target. A monotone upper envelope restores control but can yield conservative sets when the original loss is far from monotone.
cases.methods: With n calibration loss functions and upper bound B, conformal risk control chooses the smallest parameter lambda satisfying [n R_n(lambda) + B]/(n + 1) <= alpha, where R_n is their average. If none qualifies, it uses the maximum parameter, whose loss must already be at most alpha. The correction reserves room for an unseen loss as large as B instead of treating the calibration average as the test risk. The proof introduces an oracle that applies the target to the average of all n + 1 losses. The implementable choice is at least as large as the oracle's; non-increasing losses therefore make it no riskier. Conditional on the multiset of loss functions, exchangeability identifies the oracle's expected test loss with that full average, and right-continuity ensures the threshold is attained. Together, these steps establish finite-sample expected-risk control.
cases.results: The application results support near-target calibration of graded error, while showing variation across data splits. At a false-negative-rate target of 0.1, polyp segmentation yielded mean risk 0.0987 and standard deviation 0.0114 over 1,000 random splits, each using 1,000 calibration images and 781 evaluation images. MS COCO multilabel classification yielded mean risk 0.0996 and standard deviation 0.0052 at the same target over 1,000 splits, with 4,000 calibration and 1,000 evaluation images per split. Both means are close to the requested level, but this does not imply that every split or image satisfies the threshold. Segmentation had greater dispersion; because the tasks and calibration sizes differ, the comparison does not isolate the effect of calibration size. The nonmonotone counterexample supplies the complementary boundary: the unmodified rule can produce expected loss arbitrarily near B despite a lower target, so successful calibration on these monotone losses cannot justify removing that assumption.
cases.notes: Revision keeps the finite-sample upper guarantee, the separately qualified sharp lower bound, and the nonmonotone failure. Evidence: Theorems 1-2, Propositions 1-2, and segmentation/MS COCO split statistics. Standard deviations measure split-to-split risk variation, not confidence intervals or training-seed variation. The multilabel prose mentions false positives although the equation and figure concern false negatives. The QA threshold direction and shift extension's monotonicity wording need reconciliation with the theorem's non-increasing convention; neither is used to strengthen the central claim.

cases.abstract: Refitting a prediction model and its score quantiles does not necessarily restore conformal coverage when the data distribution changes. Adaptive conformal inference updates a miscoverage parameter from each newly observed coverage error: a miss lowers the parameter to favor larger sets, whereas a covered response reverses the adjustment. Summing this feedback recursion turns cumulative miscoverage error into a difference between bounded calibration levels, yielding a distribution-free finite-horizon bound and convergence of long-run empirical miscoverage to the target. This controls accumulated errors, not coverage at every time point. A hidden Markov analysis also provides concentration and approximate marginal-coverage bounds with fixed scores and quantiles, stationary initialization, and additional regularity conditions. Stock-volatility forecasting and time-zone-ordered county-vote prediction show smaller local coverage departures than fixed-level calibration. However, replacing normalized volatility scores with unnormalized absolute errors produces much wider swings, revealing that adaptation does not remove sensitivity to score design. The step size balances responsiveness to shifting calibration requirements against volatility in the parameter, and updates require a response at each time point.
cases.methods: Let alpha be the target miscoverage rate and alpha_t the parameter specifying the score threshold Q_t(1 - alpha_t). After the response is observed, update alpha_{t+1} = alpha_t + gamma(alpha - err_t), where err_t indicates a miss and gamma > 0. A miss lowers alpha_t, raising the threshold for a fixed quantile function; a covered response reverses this adjustment. Summing the recursion gives average miscoverage minus alpha as (alpha_1 - alpha_{T+1})/(gamma T). With alpha_1 in [0, 1], non-decreasing quantiles extended to yield full or empty sets outside their probability range keep alpha_t in [-gamma, 1 + gamma]. Bounded calibration levels therefore make the discrepancy vanish as T grows, without specifying a model of the shift. This guarantee concerns accumulated errors, however: extreme sets are permitted, and short-window coverage need not follow.
cases.results: The volatility comparisons distinguish the benefit of adaptive calibration from the effect of score design. With normalized errors and step size 0.005, adaptive coverage in 500-day windows stayed near the 90% target, with fluctuations comparable to the plotted Bernoulli reference. Fixed-level calibration showed larger departures, including Fannie Mae's undercoverage during the 2008 crisis. Both methods used rolling 1,250-day GARCH fits and score quantiles, so refitting alone did not prevent the fixed method's failure. Switching to unnormalized absolute errors produced much wider adaptive coverage swings, showing that feedback did not remove sensitivity to score design. The four displayed stocks were selected from twelve for conspicuous fixed-method failures. In the county-vote experiment, time-zone ordering with randomization within zones yielded fixed-method troughs around zone changes, whereas adaptive calibration maintained approximately 90% local coverage in 300-county windows. These comparisons support local correction under the tested drift constructions, not guaranteed pointwise coverage or shorter intervals.
cases.notes: Revision connects the feedback recursion to accumulated-error control and uses the score contrast to qualify local performance. Evidence: Proposition 4.1, Theorems 4.1-4.2, and Figures 1-3. Bernoulli curves are visual references, not significance tests. County time-zone ordering approximates reporting drift, not the actual election-night sequence. The stronger theory assumes fixed fitted functions and stationary initialization, unlike the rolling-refit examples. The stock formula uses centered 500-day windows despite prose describing recent history, so no trailing-window claim is made.
